etymology: English: the paragraph at the back of an agreement that decides how a signatory may leave it - notice, survival, and price.
effect: Turns an exit into a scheduled act with a bill attached: notice in writing, a published list of the obligations that survive the withdrawal, and a successor agreement that names what leaving costs.
costs: Negotiating leverage, because a state that prices its own exit has admitted it might use it.
failure: The clause that sets a notice period and nothing else - twelve months of waiting, then the same exit with a cleaner headline.
tell: A notice period with a date on it
A list of obligations that survive the signature
Allies who price the exit into the next agreement

confused_with.tell: The sunset clause gives a power a date; the withdrawal clause gives an exit a price, and publishes it before anyone leaves.

senses: The clause that makes withdrawal a procedure rather than an announcement: a period of notice, a statement of what survives the exit, and a schedule of what the departing party still owes.

It works because the benefit of an agreement is paid over decades and the cost of leaving is paid once, in a news cycle. Moving the cost into the text - a notice period the market can read, obligations that outlive the signature - makes the arbitrage visible while it is being proposed instead of after it is done.
example: *"The **withdrawal clause** bought the other parties a year of notice and a list of agreements that would outlive the government that left; the announcement ran three minutes and the bill ran four years."*
